pharm: Dose-dependent agonist at dopaminergic, beta-1, and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors; increases cardiac output and, at higher doses, vascular resistance.

summary: Dopamine hydrochloride is a catecholamine given by IV infusion to improve hemodynamic status in shock (distributive shock or shock from reduced cardiac output). Its receptor effects are dose-dependent: lower rates favor beta-1 inotropy and renal/mesenteric vasodilation, higher rates produce alpha-mediated vasoconstriction. Hypovolemia, acidosis, and hypoxia should be corrected first. Extravasation can cause ischemic tissue necrosis; treat with local phentolamine.
indications: Improvement of hemodynamic status in patients in distributive shock or shock due to reduced cardiac output

dosage.d: Start 2-5 mcg/kg/min as a continuous IV infusion
dosage.n: Correct hypovolemia, acidosis, and hypoxia first; use an infusion pump

dosage.d: Increase in 5-10 mcg/kg/min increments based on hemodynamic response and tolerability
dosage.n: Titrate to blood pressure, urine output, and cardiac output

dosage.d: Up to but not more than 50 mcg/kg/min

admin: Administer into a large vein, preferably central, with an infusion pump in a monitored/ICU setting
Correct hypovolemia, acidosis, and hypoxia before initiation
Inspect for drug incompatibilities; dopamine is inactivated in alkaline solutions
Check infusion site frequently; treat extravasation promptly with phentolamine infiltration
moa: Dopamine activates dopamine D1/D2, beta-1, and alpha-1 receptors in a dose-dependent manner. At low infusion rates dopaminergic and beta-1 effects predominate, increasing renal and mesenteric blood flow and cardiac contractility/output; at higher rates alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction increases systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure. It is the metabolic precursor of norepinephrine.

relative: Occlusive vascular disease (atherosclerosis, arterial embolism, Raynaud disease) - risk of ischemia
Concurrent MAOI therapy (reduce dopamine dose substantially)

preg: There are limited human data; use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: There are no data on presence in human milk; given critical-care use and rapid metabolism, maternal benefit generally outweighs theoretical risk.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment; titrate to hemodynamic response. Maintaining perfusion supports renal function; routine low-dose dopamine for renal protection is not recommended.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment; titrate to response.

major: MAO inhibitors (markedly potentiate and prolong dopamine effect - reduce initial dose to about one-tenth)
Cyclopropane / halogenated anesthetics (myocardial sensitization - serious arrhythmias)
moderate: Phenytoin IV (hypotension and bradycardia when given during dopamine infusion)
minor: Diuretics (additive increase in urine output at low doses)
interactions.diagnostics: Peripheral vasoconstriction at higher doses may affect perfusion-dependent measurements.

serious: Extravasation causing tissue ischemia and necrosis
Peripheral/digital ischemia and gangrene with prolonged high-dose use

monitoring: Cardiac output and filling pressures where available
counsel: This medicine is given by infusion in intensive/critical care
Blood pressure and heart rhythm are monitored continuously
The IV site is checked often because leakage can damage tissue
Report pain, burning, or skin color change at the infusion site
pk: Effect ends within about 10 minutes of stopping the infusion
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light; do not use if darker than slightly yellow or discolored
pearls: Receptor effects are dose-dependent: low-dose beta/dopaminergic (inotropy, splanchnic flow), high-dose alpha (vasoconstriction)
EXTRAVASATION causes ischemic necrosis - prefer a central line; treat leakage with local phentolamine infiltration
Correct hypovolemia, acidosis, and hypoxia before and during use
Contraindicated in pheochromocytoma; reduce dose ~10-fold with MAOIs
Inactivated in alkaline solutions; do not mix with sodium bicarbonate
missed: Not applicable - administered as a continuously titrated IV infusion by clinicians, not on a fixed dosing schedule.
overdose: Overdose presents as excessive sympathomimetic effect: marked hypertension, tachyarrhythmias, and intense vasoconstriction with peripheral ischemia. Because of the very short half-life, reducing or stopping the infusion usually reverses effects rapidly; persistent severe hypertension can be treated with a short-acting alpha-blocker (phentolamine).
